notes:
Task and constraints: Build the lexicographically largest length-k sequence from two arrays while preserving order.
Idea: Choose how many digits to take from each array, then merge their best subsequences.
Technique and why it applies: max_digit greedily removes smaller earlier digits; delete_digit builds best subsequences for several lengths; merge chooses the lexicographically larger remaining suffix at each step.
Invariant: The result must use exactly k digits, and each chosen subsequence preserves its source order.
Edge cases: Ties during merging require comparing full remaining sequences, not only first digits.
Complexity: The stated complexity is nuanced; repeated list slicing and suffix comparisons can push work toward O(k(m+n+k^2)). Storage includes subsequences and intermediate lists. Author labels are approximate.

Task and constraints: Determine whether a positive integer is a power of three.
Idea: Compare the logarithm base three with its nearest integer after rounding.
Technique and why it applies: The code calls log(n,3) twice and rounds to nine decimal places, attempting to test whether the exponent is integral.
Invariant: Powers of three have integer logarithms, but floating-point approximations can be inaccurate.
Edge cases: Nonpositive inputs return false; log is not imported in the snippet and must be defined.
Complexity: O(1) time and space in the arithmetic model, but floating-point rounding is fragile. No author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Count subarrays whose sums lie within the inclusive interval [lower, upper].
Idea: Use prefix sums and shift the acceptable interval as each starting element is removed.
Technique and why it applies: acc stores prefix sums; each iteration counts entries within the shifted bounds, then pops the first prefix and shifts lower and upper by the current number.
Invariant: The shifted bounds transform prefix-sum checks into subarray-sum checks for the next starting position.
Edge cases: The logic scans the remaining prefix list repeatedly and mutates acc; accumulate is not imported in the shown code.
Complexity: Repeated scans and pop(0) make time O(n^2); storage is O(n). No author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the longest strictly increasing path in a matrix using horizontal or vertical moves.
Idea: Memoize depth-first search results for each cell.
Technique and why it applies: dfs rejects out-of-bounds or non-increasing moves, then explores four neighbors with the current value as the next lower bound.
Invariant: A cell's longest increasing suffix depends only on its own value and neighboring values, so memoization by cell is valid.
Edge cases: The code assumes a nonempty matrix and accesses matrix[0] immediately; empty input would fail.
Complexity: Each cell is memoized once with four edges, giving O(mn) time and O(mn) space. No labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Return the longest strictly increasing path length in a matrix.
Idea: Memoize a DFS result for each cell and explore four directions.
Technique and why it applies: The helper returns cached lengths or recursively considers neighbors with greater values, storing the longest length in max_lengths.
Invariant: Each cell's cached value is the longest increasing path starting there.
Edge cases: The matrix constraints imply nonempty dimensions; the cached table uses zero to mean uncomputed.
Complexity: O(mn) time and O(mn) space, matching labels.

Task and constraints: Find the longest increasing path in a matrix without revisiting cells along a path.
Idea: Use topological layers: count incoming edges from smaller neighbors and process local minima first.
Technique and why it applies: The code builds an indegree matrix and processes cells in layers, moving to larger neighbors as their indegrees drop.
Invariant: Each layer advances one step along any increasing path; the number of layers equals the longest path length.
Edge cases: An empty matrix returns zero. The approach avoids recursion and uses a queue/frontier plus indegree storage.
Complexity: O(mn) time and O(mn) space. No author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum numbers to add so every value from one through n is representable as a subset sum.
Idea: Track the contiguous range of sums already representable and patch any gap.
Technique and why it applies: The method appends n+1 to nums, starts with coverage sum=1, and either adds a patch of sum+1 or extends coverage using nums[t].
Invariant: If values through sum are representable, adding sum+1 extends coverage to twice sum plus one.
Edge cases: It mutates nums by appending n+1; the algorithm assumes sorted positive input. Empty input needs careful handling.
Complexity: The greedy scan is O(n+patches) time and O(1) extra space aside from mutation; no labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Compute the minimum patches needed to represent every sum from one through n.
Idea: Maintain the largest continuously reachable sum and patch when the next number leaves a gap.
Technique and why it applies: Before using x, while reachable<x-1 it adds reachable+1 as a patch; then x extends the range.
Invariant: If sums through reachable are possible, patching reachable+1 doubles the reachable interval.
Edge cases: It returns early when coverage reaches n; input is expected sorted and positive.
Complexity: O(n+log n) time in the standard bound and O(1) extra space. No time label supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of patches to cover all sums up to n.
Idea: Track the smallest missing sum and consume input values that do not create a gap.
Technique and why it applies: If nums[i] is at most miss, it extends coverage by nums[i]; otherwise a patch of miss doubles coverage and increments patch.
Invariant: All sums below miss are already representable; the next missing value determines the optimal patch.
Edge cases: The loop stops once miss exceeds n; sorted positive input is assumed.
Complexity: O(n+log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. No time label supplied.

Task and constraints: Determine the fewest patches needed so every sum from one to n is constructible.
Idea: Extend a contiguous reachable-sum interval, patching gaps before using each input number.
Technique and why it applies: For each x not exceeding n, the code patches while reachable<x-1, then adds x; afterward it patches until coverage reaches n.
Invariant: The invariant is that every sum from one through reachable can be formed.
Edge cases: Values above n are irrelevant and terminate input processing; nums is not modified.
Complexity: O(n+log n) time and O(1) extra space. No time label supplied.

Task and constraints: Validate whether a comma-separated preorder serialization represents a binary tree.
Idea: Track available child slots, starting with one slot for the root.
Technique and why it applies: Each non-null token consumes one slot and creates two, represented by counter+=1; each '#' consumes one slot by decrementing the counter.
Invariant: A valid serialization ends with exactly zero open slots and never runs out before the final token.
Edge cases: The condition rejects exhausted slots before the last token; final counter equality catches leftover or negative slots.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) storage for split tokens. No author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Check whether preorder serialization of a binary tree is valid.
Idea: Split tokens incrementally and track available child slots without allocating a token list.
Technique and why it applies: split_iter yields comma-delimited tokens; the main scan updates slot count for null and non-null nodes and rejects invalid slot states.
Invariant: A non-null node consumes one slot and adds two, while '#' only consumes one.
Edge cases: The final token must leave exactly zero slots; malformed empty tokens are also processed as tokens.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space beyond token iteration, matching labels.

Task and constraints: Determine whether an array contains a strictly increasing subsequence of length three.
Idea: Maintain the smallest first and second values seen so far.
Technique and why it applies: A value replaces first if no larger than it, otherwise replaces second if no larger than second; a value larger than both completes a triplet.
Invariant: first and second represent increasingly larger candidate values from earlier positions.
Edge cases: Equal values replace candidates rather than extending the sequence, preserving strict increase.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space. No author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Generalize increasing-triplet detection to a strictly increasing subsequence of length k.
Idea: Maintain minimal tail values and binary-search where each number can extend the candidate subsequence.
Technique and why it applies: The helper initializes k-1 tails to infinity, finds the lower-bound index, returns true if the index reaches k-1, otherwise updates that tail.
Invariant: The tails array tracks the smallest possible ending values for increasing subsequences of each shorter length.
Edge cases: For k=3 it checks for a triplet; equal values replace rather than extend.
Complexity: O(n log k) time and O(k) space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Return whether any three values form a strictly increasing subsequence in order.
Idea: Track the smallest first value and two later increasing candidates.
Technique and why it applies: Each number updates the first threshold, then the second, or returns true if it exceeds both.
Invariant: The candidates preserve the possibility of extending a subsequence using later values.
Edge cases: Equal values replace existing thresholds and do not satisfy strict increase.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space. No author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Determine whether a path formed by successive segment lengths crosses itself.
Idea: Check the three geometric crossing patterns that can first arise from the fourth segment onward.
Technique and why it applies: For each i, compare current and earlier distances for simple crossing, overlap with the segment three steps back, and spiral crossing with the segment five steps back.
Invariant: Each condition encodes a known local configuration sufficient to detect a crossing.
Edge cases: Fewer than four segments cannot cross; later checks are guarded by i>=4 and i>=5.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space. No author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Detect whether the sequence of orthogonal segment lengths crosses itself.
Idea: Check the initial special loop pattern, then scan later segments using geometric inequalities.
Technique and why it applies: The method tests the special overlap case first, then applies the three local crossing conditions to each new segment.
Invariant: Only a bounded set of previous segment lengths is needed to determine a new crossing.
Edge cases: Paths with fewer than four segments cannot cross; conditions are guarded by index.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Find pairs of word indices whose concatenation forms a palindrome.
Idea: Use a reverse-word map and test palindromic prefixes and suffixes.
Technique and why it applies: For each word, the code shrinks prefix/suffix views and looks up the reversed complementary substring, storing ordered index pairs in a set.
Invariant: A split is valid when one side is palindromic and the other side matches a reversed word.
Edge cases: The set deduplicates pairs; duplicate words in the map overwrite earlier indices, which may miss pairs involving repeated identical words.
Complexity: Runtime depends on repeated slicing and palindrome checks, often O(nk^2); space is O(total input plus output). No labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Find word pairs whose concatenation is a palindrome, using a trie of reversed words.
Idea: Insert each reversed word and search matching suffixes while checking remaining prefixes for palindromicity.
Technique and why it applies: TrieNode.find walks the input backward and emits a pair when the remaining prefix is a palindrome and the matched word is different.
Invariant: The trie prefix represents a reversed word suffix; palindrome checks validate the unmatched part.
Edge cases: The implementation includes Manacher preprocessing for each word and may produce multiple candidate pairs; output size can be large.
Complexity: Time depends on total characters and palindrome processing; space includes trie and prefix/suffix indexes. The stated O(nk^2) space is plausible as a coarse bound.

Task and constraints: Find all pairs of words whose concatenation forms a palindrome.
Idea: Index words by length and test palindromic prefixes and suffixes against reversed substrings.
Technique and why it applies: For each word split position, the code tests the remaining suffix or prefix for palindromicity and looks up the reversed complementary string in the matching length bucket.
Invariant: A valid pair consists of a palindromic side plus a reversed matching word on the other side.
Edge cases: The dictionary stores one index per exact word, so duplicate identical words overwrite prior indices and may omit valid pairs.
Complexity: Time is proportional to word splits times palindrome checks and lookups; space is O(total characters plus output). No labels supplied.
